title: ‘We will become cyborgs!’ Peter Gabriel on bonobo ape duets, building a Jurassic Park for plants – and why AI will make great music
summary: From sampling to streaming, the rock legend has always been in thrall to technology – but is superintelligence a step too far? Back with an epic new album, he unpacks his remarkable ideas Peter Gabriel asks me to fetch my laptop: he wants to show me a video of himself playing a keyboard duet with a bonobo called Kanzi. In fairness, said footage is, as Gabriel suggests, “extraordinary”. Working with primatologist Sue Savage-Rumbaugh, who developed a means of communicating with bonobos involving sign language and a speech-synthesis keyboard, Gabriel plays droning chords on a synthesiser while Kanzi picks out complementary notes on a piano. “Look, she likes that note, which is a ninth, and then she finds the octave,” he enthuses as the video plays. “There’s a real musicality there.” It is all deeply unlikely, but it seems the perfect illustration of how easily a conversation with Gabriel can go wildly – if fascinatingly – off-piste. I’ve only been in his company for 10 minutes, long enough to ask a solitary question about his epic new album o\i: its 13 tracks last nearly 90 minutes, the result, he suggests, of a longstanding interest in African music “which made me realise that a song could last as long as a song could last”, and of “being old enough to think ‘fuck it’, really”. For anyone who feels that an hour and a half of exquisitely arranged, beautifully produced, occasionally deeply strange art rock – its sound shapeshifting from the folk-flecked A Hard Lesson to the glowing pop hues of Till Your Mind Is Shining – is too meagre an offering, it arrives in two versions: a “dark” mix by US producer Tchad Blake and a “bright” version that’s the handiwork of Mike “Spike” Stent, famed for working with everyone from U2 and Madonna to Frank Ocean and Harry Styles. title: A single pull request could have handed attackers the keys to Microsoft’s software supply chain
summary: The most dangerous actor in a software supply chain may now be an automated script with powerful credentials and no idea where it’s sending them. Researchers from pen-testing company Cycode have discovered a now patched critical zero-click supply chain vulnerability in the open-source Windows Package Manager (WinGet), which sits on billions of devices worldwide. A single pull request could have tricked Microsoft’s internal tooling into freely handing over a moderator’s GitHub access token, with no phishing, no malware, no moderator clicking or approval required. There is currently no evidence that the flaw has been exploited in the wild. But it serves as a cautionary tale for enterprises that the automation they trust is becoming an attacker entry point, and package repositories are particularly enticing targets. “Package registries have become the highest-profile target in the software supply chain,” Moriel Harush , Cycode security research lead, wrote in a blog post . “Compromise a single maintainer, and you reach everyone who trusts them. Compromise the gatekeepers, and you reach the entire ecosystem.” Whatever the employee can do, the attacker can do WinGet is Microsoft’s free, open source command line tool that helps users discover, install, upgrade, configure, and remove apps. It exists on more than 1.4 billion active devices running Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server 2025. WinGet’s catalog is a public GitHub repository , and its gatekeeper, so to speak, is a small, official group of Microsoft moderators who review a constant stream of community pull requests and proposed changes. By default, WinGet installations on every Windows machine trust the actions those keepers take. The hole is in the moderators’ own internal triage tool. This PowerShell helper attached the moderator’s secret GitHub Personal Access Token (PAT) to any HTTP request, without checking who owned that address. title: AI coding agents need a safe place to work; Eclipse is building the sandbox to give it to them
summary: AI coding tools are moving beyond copilots that make suggestions to independent, autonomous agents that execute terminal commands, write and modify software, run tests, and install dependencies. This means they need the freedom to move around on their own, but that is inherently dangerous; agents with little oversight or unrestricted access can make changes they aren’t supposed to, expose credentials and other sensitive information, or take other unintended actions, as vendors have discovered the hard way . To help move the bar on these security and governance challenges , the Eclipse Foundation has launched Eclipse Enclave 1.0, an AI sandbox and runtime. Developers can use the vendor-neutral platform to test various autonomous AI coding tools in isolated environments, with explicitly defined access to files, credentials, and networks. The alternative has been to keep the agent on a “very short leash,” which requires developers to approve every action, said Thabang Mashologu , CMO and head of products at the Eclipse Foundation. And at that point, you’re losing a lot of the productivity benefits of having an autonomous agent in the first place. “Ultimately, developers shouldn’t have to choose between agent productivity and security,” he said. More independent work, less supervision The Eclipse Foundation is a non-profit chartered in the EU that supports and governs more than 450 open source software projects. That now includes Eclipse Enclave 1.0, which currently supports Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, GitHub Copilot CLI, Pi, and Eclipse Theia. Its extensible architecture allows for additional tool integration. Developers can run agent sessions in isolated containers, allowing them to work independently but with limited access to sensitive files and resources. Built-in mechanisms help protect API keys and OAuth tokens for third-party services. title: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)
summary: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube) Claire Vo runs ChatPRD , an AI platform that helps product managers "turn an idea into a spec". The product has been live since the GPT-4 era, and Claire has been building it in public for much of that time. In this YouTube video (see also the accompanying Twitter post ) Claire describes the flood of token fraud she has seen from groups abusing the product's free trial, sometimes just to get free AI usage but often to resell tokens or run other commercial enterprises on top of the ChatPRD agent. I am funding a international Roblox and Fortnite map studio. They run a loop of free trials and promo codes and then tunnel to my agent and use it to build Roblox and Fortnite maps. Apparently one of the common prompts Claire saw running through her agent involved SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles! Presumably the token scammers are using that to help sniff the underlying models - different model families have a definite signature, and I've used it like this in the past to try and guess the identity of stealth preview models on platforms like OpenRouter. Claire is winding down her free trials entirely, which sadly looks like the right decision in the face of this abuse. Tags: youtube , ai , generative-ai , llms , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , ai-misuse

title: 21 ways Gemini can genuinely be useful on Android
summary: Google’s Gemini chatbot gets a bit of a bad rap as an Android assistant — and, let’s be honest: It’s easy to see why. Google rushed Gemini out of the gates long before it was ready . It crippled the perfectly fine Google Assistant experience , and even with all the progress over time, Gemini still can’t do everything Assistant did in terms of day-to-day device basics — despite having now fully replaced Assistant and sent that service to the Google Graveyard . Beyond that, Gemini can be complicated and confusing , with its many models and cryptically coded options. It’s being shoved in our faces at every possible opportunity in a move reminiscent of a certain other much-maligned Google service . And, most troubling of all, it’s being positioned as an all-purpose answer machine when it gets answers wildly wrong anywhere from 5 to 20% of the time . Just like all the other generative AI chatbots of the moment, in other words, it’s a steaming hot mess — even if it’s all anyone in the tech industry wants to talk about these days. But the problem with Gemini (and other similar systems) is less the technology itself and more the way its maker insists on framing it. These large-language model mechanisms just aren’t good at understanding context or offering consistently reliable answers. They shouldn’t be set up to serve as replacements for search. They get stuff wrong shockingly often, for cryin’ out loud. It’s par for the course with the underlying technology, and it’s just plain silly to see the results. (Seriously: The hits keep comin’ — and comin’ , and comin’ , and…well, you get the idea .) They are , however, useful in other ways — namely when it comes to more subjective, mundane sorts of tasks where context, judgment, and a lack of flat-out fabricating aren’t required. title: Apple doesn’t need the smartest AI agent. It needs the most trusted one
summary: When MacPaw , Proton , Google , OpenAI , Anthropic , and others are doing it, it’s not really such a surprise that Apple is working to introduce agentic AI tools in Siri and Apple Intelligence. The wider question is how the company plans to deploy these tools — how it will deliver the maximum convenience at the least possible cost to user privacy and data integrity. Some of those answers are already easy to speculate on. Apple has already put some of the building blocks in place, including the recent move to make consumers think more deeply when providing AI agents with Full Disk Access . Convenience versus control I know some competitors are complaining about this, but frankly I think user privacy outweighs commercial convenience — users should have a conscious choice, which Apple delivers. “Addressing this is critical,” Apple told developers . “As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy.” Apple’s decision to make it possible to confine agents to folder access also speaks volumes, as it shows us how it will probably choose to manage its own agents. Siri AI may have contextual understanding of everything, which can inform Siri Agents, but the agents themselves will have but limited access to your data. They gain contextual direction from the user and from Siri AI but are limited to the proscribed folders and files when it comes to acting. Making the cloud sweat a little Some tasks are harder than others. The really hard tasks will still lean into Apple’s Private Cloud Compute , and I think the company will try to introduce Secure Exclave into that relationship, so even the most complex task instructions only upload the minimum quantity of your information required to get a task done. title: Nadella: Here’s why Microsoft offered buyouts to 60,000 employees
summary: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella commented at the New York Times Dealbook Summit on why the company offered severance packages to approximately 60,000 employees in October to encourage them to voluntarily leave their jobs. According to Nadella, it’s not that AI will replace programmers, for example, but rather that their roles are fundamentally changing. As an example, he cited a development team working on Cowork in Microsoft 365 that consists of only 11 people. “They’re building a software factory that builds the product. They’re not building the product themselves,” said Nadella, as reported by TechCrunch . He believes that the same trend could affect virtually every profession. But the transition will be particularly challenging for an established company like Microsoft, which wasn’t built from the ground up around AI. According to Nadella, the changes may be difficult for some employees, and the voluntary separation offer was intended to give employees the opportunity to choose whether they want to be part of the transition or leave the company. This article originally appeared on Computer Sweden .

title: The AI boom is forecast to increase data center emissions by 70% by 2030
summary: A new report from the International Energy Agency (IEA) warns that electricity consumption by the world’s data centers is expected to nearly double in the next four years, according to The Guardian . The world’s existing data centers currently have a capacity of about 120 gigawatts. According to the IEA, an additional 120 gigawatts could be added by 2030. The expansion of artificial intelligence is expected to account for about 75% of that increase. At the same time, carbon dioxide emissions from data centers risk increasing by 70%. This is despite the fact that data center companies are among the world’s largest corporate buyers of renewable energy. In the US, natural gas is projected to account for about 60% of data centers’ electricity supply by 2030. In China, however, coal-fired power is expected to account for about half of data centers’ electricity supply. IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol also warns that the energy market is in a historically uncertain situation following the war in the Middle East. title: From a medical report to a checked record: what can rules verify?
summary: A report can mention a finding without saying that it is present now. It may describe an earlier examination, deny an observation or leave a question unresolved. Turning those sentences into a database requires more than finding familiar words. This article follows an original, fictional example through a proposed extraction, explicit checks and a decision to retain uncertainty. A clinical research study provides a bounded comparison, while standards for data validation and provenance help distinguish a well-formed record from a true statement about the world. The central question is what a deterministic rule can establish when the text it receives is incomplete or its interpretation is wrong. The answer matters for research collections built from medical reports: a reproducible check can expose an inconsistency, but it cannot replace the evidence that the record is supposed to represent.
author: The Bible of AI

title: The driving model proposes a move. Which rule can stop it?
summary: A vehicle can recognise the road and still propose a manoeuvre that should not be executed. This article examines the boundary between a learned driving policy and a rule that can restrict its commands. A small, fully specified example shows how acceleration and steering limits change a proposal; a second calculation shows why the same rule becomes unreliable when its assumptions about braking are wrong. Research on symbolic shields provides the foundation, while a recent simulation study illustrates both the benefits and costs of intervention. Fewer collisions in some scenarios can come with longer delays and lower performance elsewhere. The question is what has actually been checked: a command, a model of the environment, or behaviour on a real road. These are different levels of evidence, and the distinction matters when learning is used inside a physical system.
author: The Bible of AI

title: When an AI draws another line, what makes the proof valid?
summary: Adding a line to a triangle can reveal a route to a proof. It can also create a convincing picture that establishes nothing. This article follows a simple geometric construction to distinguish a useful proposal from a justified conclusion. The reader can check each step: what is given, what is constructed, which rule applies and what remains to be shown. A deliberately incorrect shortcut reveals why a missing assumption cannot be repaired by repeating the same answer. AlphaGeometry2 provides the research context for this distinction between learned suggestions and symbolic deduction. Its published evaluation is read with its actual denominator and the limits of its mathematical language. The available implementation also makes it necessary to distinguish testing a deductive component from reproducing an entire system. The question for this collection is how learning can assist reasoning while the conditions for accepting a result remain explicit and open to examination.

title: Agentic AI repeats same old enterprise adoption cycle
summary: The pitch sounded perfect. A large regional distributor needed to build a new sales transaction management system. The goal was straightforward: automate parts of order intake, discount approvals, exception handling, customer communications, and inventory checks. It was not a trivial system, but it was also something the industry had built before. Then the vendor presentations began. Every software provider seemed to have a new agentic AI story. Their platforms had agents that could make decisions, orchestrate workflows, interpret customer intent, route exceptions, and learn from business context. One vendor described its offering as a common LLM brain that could make decisions as if the company had hired 10,000 experts, except those experts were not on the payroll. That line was from an actual sales pitch, and it landed well in the boardroom. The company decided to go agentic. The architecture would use AI agents to manage decision flows, invoke tools, check policies, interact with enterprise systems, and escalate only when needed. It looked modern. It looked strategic. It looked like the future. Then reality arrived. Building the system required far more integration work than expected. Each agent needed access to clean data, governed APIs, business rules, security controls, observability, exception handling, and human override mechanisms. The team had to build guardrails around decisions, logging around reasoning, test harnesses for unpredictable outcomes, and new operational processes for things traditional systems handled more predictably. Costs ballooned. Security reviews took longer. Operational complexity increased. The project ultimately ran fine once in production, but six months later, the company realized the uncomfortable truth: the system cost roughly 20 times more than a traditional architecture would have cost when all supporting complexity was included, and it delivered about the same ROI. title: TheoPhysEval: Assessing AI agents at autonomous theoretical physics problem solving
summary: How much of a theoretical physicist's calculational work can an AI agent perform without guidance? TheoPhysEval puts five agents to work on 50 research-level problems spanning 11 areas of physics, from classical dynamics to quantum field theory and gravity. The strongest tested configuration, GPT-6-Astra with Codex, obtains accepted final answers on 49 problems with Internet access and 46 without it. The study offers a detailed view of what these systems can calculate, where they fail and how much their use costs. Its results also raise a deeper question: what distinguishes a correct answer from a trustworthy scientific contribution? Each configuration was evaluated once, the principal scores concern final answers, and the experiment does not include a matched comparison with human specialists. Those boundaries make the paper particularly useful for understanding both the promise of AI-assisted theoretical research and the further evidence needed before calculation can be equated with autonomous discovery.
